title: Bobby Hackett tracks and choosing material for festival records
summary: Working with Bobby is a pleasure; she explains why few of her new songs appear on festival albums and why she picks uncommon material.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Well anyway, on this album from Decmeber of '69, Manassas Jazz Festival, which is No. 112 on the Fat Cat label, you not only have your -- what has become, I supposed, your standard accompanying group, the Tommy Gwaltney Trio or quartet, rather.
But on two tracks, you're favored with accompaniment by Bobby Hackett which is a --
Yeah.

Which gives it a nice touch.

It's always a pleasure to work with Bobby. And as I said before, these things -- they're recorded and you don't know how Fat Cat is going to put them out. On this particular album, he has Bobby, Vic and Maxine. And there's some selections featuring Bobby, and some featuring Vic. And I've got -- well five out of ten of these selections are vocals with me doing the vocals. And I said earlier, also, that you're not working with same group all the time when you're doing a festival. And there is a possibility that these also were recorded at different times of the festival. Either a Friday, Saturday or a Sunday. So, I really don't -- you never know until these things come out.
Yeah. What's going to

appear and what's not.

Apparently, at the same -- First of all, according to letter I received him -- I inquired about what additional material he may have on you -- if my information is correct, you also sang at this December festival, "If I Had A Ribbon Bow."
Yeah.
And that's come out on a different album again.
Right.
No. 117 on the same label.
Right.
Well, one thing -- when I do the jazz festival, I usually do the same songs each time, you know, over the years.
So, it's very difficult for him to include many selections of mine without repeating. So this cuts down on the albums I'll be making for Fat Cat.
But that's what happens for me today. It's

not that easy in the first place to select new material unless you are deliberately going to make a record. You know, make an album.
In that case, you will have a tendency to include those selections in your repertoire.
And I don't like to just put things on --

When you have to make an album, you take into consideration you're going to do about ten selections minimum, you're not going to include all of these in your repertoire. You wouldn't havetime to sing them when you're working.
So,-- and I like to feel that I put a lot of work in trying to select the right songs. And you just can't sit down and do this every day.
Are you saying that you might've been happier making more studio recordings than --
No, no. I like it this way, because --
You see, in selecting a tune even for albums or for live performances, you like to do things

So, at least if you do what everybody is not doing, you're going to at least be the first with it, which is very important. Otherwise, you're just singing songs to be singing, and doing what's currently popular. And then you get in the situation where you have to keep looking for new material. So far as I'm concerned, there is not that much good material being turned out constantly, which is good -- which is the way it should be. Because otherwise -- I mean, it's enough like a mill as it is, you know. The way that the publishers have to turn out music. But in order to be, say, individual, you have to pick out material that suits you, material that you feel that you can do well, that you can interpret, and things that you like to do. I can't see myself just doing songs just to be doing them because they're number one on the hit parade.
